title: Misrouted canary traffic due to routing table drift; rollback automation & postmortem
creator: Marco Nguyen
description: During a staged rollout of model v4.2 to 5% canary traffic, an unexpected drift in the canary routing table caused 100% of traffic for a small subset of customers to be routed to the canary cohort. This produced a spike in latency and a small increase in token cost; automated rollback attempts partially failed due to a race with autoscaling cleanup. This ticket captures the incident timeline, root cause analysis, mitigation steps taken, and concrete action items to prevent recurrence.
timeline: 2026-03-06T14:05Z - Start: Rollout started; config: route 5% traffic to model v4.2 via canary-routing-policy #CR-91
2026-03-06T14:12Z - Alert: Latency SLO breach on shard eu-west-1-a for model v4.2 (p95 latency +200ms)
2026-03-06T14:15Z - Pager: Ops on-call paged (Aisha) after error rate grew to 0.7% for affected tenant segment
2026-03-06T14:20Z - Investigation: Observed traffic split metric reported 5% overall but traffic heatmap showed a small set of customer IDs receiving >90% canary traffic

2026-03-06T14:28Z - Mitigation attempt: Triggered automated rollback job (rollback-job-20260306-1428). Job partially executed but failed to complete due to in-flight connection drain race with autoscaler teardown
2026-03-06T14:35Z - Manual intervention: Ops forced full rollback via control-plane API, restored routing table to previous stable version. Latency decreased toward baseline by 14:50Z
2026-03-06T15:05Z - Post-incident: Began collecting logs, saved canary routing table snapshots, and captured autoscaler and connection drain timelines
2026-03-06T18:30Z - Drafted initial incident report and notified impacted customers via CS outreach
root_cause: Routing table drift caused by a race in the rollout-service reconciliation loop: when a canary rule was created, a stale replica of the routing table used last-applied index led to duplicate entry for a small prefix of tenant IDs. The evaluation function in the canary router evaluated the duplicate entry with a stronger precedence, effectively mapping that prefix to the canary bucket. Additionally, rollback automation assumed idempotent teardown but did not account for concurrent autoscaler-triggered instance termination, which interrupted the rollback state machine leading to partial rollback failures.
mitigation: Immediate: Manual rollback to stable routing configuration and forced reconciliation of routing nodes across control-plane replicas
Short-term: Hotfix deployed to rollout-service to add optimistic locking on routing-table updates and a guard to detect duplicate prefix entries
Short-term: Updated rollback job to wait for connection drain completion and autoscaler quiesce before finalizing state
Monitoring: Added a canary-specific heatmap alert to detect skew in traffic distribution across tenant prefixes within 1 minute
Customer: Notified affected customers with timeline and applied credit for increased request cost
postmortem_summary: The incident was the result of two interacting bugs: (1) a reconciliation race that allowed duplicate/overlapping routing entries to take precedence for a tenant prefix, and (2) rollback automation that did not coordinate with the autoscaler lifecycle. Together these allowed canary traffic to concentrate on a small set of customers and prevented a clean automated rollback. No model correctness regressions were found; impact was latency/throughput and increased cost for a subset of customers. The incident was contained within ~20 minutes of detection after manual rollback. Root cause fixes and monitoring improvements are planned and in progress.
